newsitem.title: USA: Clinton admin deciding hard bank reform question.
newsitem.headline: Clinton admin deciding hard bank reform question.

text.p: Clinton administration officials, composing their own version of financial sector reform, are considering a variety of approaches to resolve one of the most controversial questions involved, a top Treasury Department official said on Wednesday.

While most in Congress and industry favor tearing down the legal barriers separating banking from other financial service sectors like insurance and securities underwriting, there is little consensus about going even further and allowing non-financial companies to own banks.
Treasury Under Secretary John Hawke said the administration is considering several possible approaches.

"There have been a number of different approaches suggested to that and we're looking at all of them," Hawke said in a speech to the thrift industry trade group America's Community Bankers. "There are some advantages and disadvantages in all of these."

Hawke mentioned several bills being considered by Congress. One bill would impose no limits on financial and non-financial companies merging. Another bill would allow financial companies to conduct 25 percent of their business in non-financial sectors.
Hawke headed an administration task force on financial sector reform that recommended allowing mixing of commercial and financial companies, people familiar with recommendations have said.
Most recently, the administration has been leaning in favor of a basket approach similiar to the Congressional proposal containing a 25 percent cap on non-financial activity, the people said.
"The signals we've seen are that they are leaning toward a basket approach," one person said.
Hawke declined to comment on the issue after his speech. "I really don't want to talk about where we stand on issues right now," he told reporters.
During the speech, Hawke criticized some who have opposed mixing banking and commerce.

"It's really unfortunate that this discussion gets mired down in a kind of sloganeering," Hawke said. "Neither the marketplace nor we have expressed any interest in trying to make the world of financial institutions safe for acquisition by industrial companies that have nothing to do with financial services," he said. "That has never been our objective."

The administration is required to submit a report by March 31 on merging the charters of banks and thrifts. Hawke said the report, which could be in the form of a legislative proposal, will include the administration's comprehensive view of financial modernization.

Some issues will not be included in the plan, however, Hawke said. For example, the plan will not take a position on whether interest should be paid to banks on demand deposits, he said. The plan will also not address deposit insurance reform, he said.
